The Chief Executive’s Report is presented to elected members at each SDCC monthly 
meeting. It forms a key part of our governance and oversight framework, supporting 
members in their role by providing timely updates on the work of the Council.
In line with Section 136(2) of the Local Government Act 2001 (as amended by the Local 
Government Reform Act 2014), the report outlines the performance of executive functions, 
the implementation of Council policy, and the delivery of services across the organisation.
This report should be read alongside updates provided to Area Committee Meetings and the 
quarterly Capital Progress Report, which together offer a comprehensive view of Council 
activity and progress.
Each edition includes:
•	Updates on how we are delivering on our Corporate Plan goals
•	Highlights of major initiatives and events
•	A visual snapshot of recent community and Council activities
The report also provides an opportunity to shine a light on areas of our work that may not 
always be in the spotlight but are vital to the day-to-day life of the county.

Climate Leadership
Innovative solar‑powered lighting installed in Bawnogue
As part of the Bawnogue district centre 
enhancement project, solar‑powered 
public lighting has been installed beneath 
high‑voltage electricity transmission pylons, 
demonstrating the effective dual use of 
pylon wayleave land. The initiative provides 
safe and reliable lighting in areas that have 
traditionally remained unlit and underused. 
The off‑grid lighting units make use of 
unobstructed solar exposure along the 
transmission corridors, generating and 
storing their own power and operating 
independently of the electricity network. 
Each unit incorporates solar panels, battery 
storage and energy‑efficient LED lighting 
within a durable, weather‑resistant housing. 
The lights activate automatically at dusk and 
switch off at dawn. 
The system has been designed in full 
compliance with safety and proximity 
requirements relating to high‑voltage 
infrastructure and has been delivered in 
coordination with ESB Networks. Installation 
required no trenching or cabling, resulting 
in minimal disruption and low ongoing 
maintenance, with battery replacement 
forming the primary routine requirement. 
This innovative approach improves safety 
and accessibility in the area while supporting 
renewable energy use and contributing to 
wider sustainable infrastructure and climate 
objectives. 
Cycle Right programme delivery across the county 
We continue to support the delivery of the 
Cycle Right programme, Ireland’s national 
standard for cycle training, as part of its 
wider objectives around road safety, active 
travel and sustainable transport. 
The programme is supported by the 
Department of Transport and the Road 
Safety Authority and is delivered locally in 
partnership with SDCC. Through a network 
of qualified and accredited instructors, 
the schools‑based programme focuses on 
developing road awareness, bike‑handling 
skills and safe on‑road cycling behaviour 
among children from an early age. 
During the first quarter of 2026, Cycle Right 
training was delivered in schools across 
several areas of the county, with a total 
of 394 students taking part. Training was 
provided in Clondalkin, Lucan, Tallaght and 
Rathfarnham, supporting consistent access 
to cycle training across communities. 
This continued delivery reflects our 
commitment to improving road safety 
outcomes, encouraging active travel 
habits from a young age and supporting 
sustainable transport choices across the 
county. 
Re‑Turn for Children’s Charities scheme 
Dedicated Re-turn for Children bins have 
been installed at our offices in County Hall 
and in Clondalkin. The fundraising initiative, 
launched in conjunction with Re-turn, 
the operator of Ireland’s Deposit Return 
Scheme, supports six national children’s 
charities. 
Instead of redeeming the 15 cent or 25 cent 
deposit, eligible empty bottles and cans can 
be placed directly into the dedicated bins 
with the deposit refunded to the initiative 
and donated to children’s charities. The 
bins are located in County Hall (main staff 
canteen and in the concourse near the main 
entrance) and in the hub canteen at our 
offices in Clondalkin. 
This scheme will benefit both the 
environment and the wider community. 
Donated containers are kept out of 
general waste and litter streams, ensuring 
high‑quality plastic and aluminium are 
recycled. This supports the circular economy 
by reducing the need for virgin materials 
and saving energy. At the same time, each 
bottle or can donated contributes directly 
to fundraising for children’s charities, 
supporting vital services and programmes 
for children across Ireland.

As part of Ireland’s commitment to 
delivering local climate action 41 
Decarbonising Zones (DZ) were established 
in a coordinated nationwide approach. 
These zones, which include urban, 
part‑urban and rural areas, cover more than 
530,000 people across all local authority 
areas. They act as testing grounds for 
locally led climate measures, including 
retrofitting, renewable energy, sustainable 
transport and biodiversity initiatives, all 
contributing towards a national target of a 
51% reduction in emissions by 2030. 
Clondalkin is designated as South Dublin’s 
Decarbonising Zone and provides a 
collaborative opportunity for the council, 
communities and local stakeholders to 
work together to reduce carbon emissions 
and build a more sustainable and resilient 
area. 
During the past year, extensive engagement 
has taken place across Clondalkin 
Clondalkin Decarbonising Zone: leading local climate action
Climate Leadership
through public surveys, local events 
and workshops involving residents, 
businesses and community organisations. 
These conversations have shaped the 
Decarbonising Zone Implementation Plan, 
which is now being finalised. 
Ahead of the publication of the plan, 
which is expected to take place in 
September, a number of initiatives have 
already progressed within the Clondalkin 
DZ. Local businesses have also been 
supported through the Climate Innovation 
Programme, delivered in partnership 
with Trinity College Dublin and Munster 
Technological University. This free 
programme focused on turning climate 
theory into practical, cost‑saving actions, 
with participants developing plans to 
reduce emissions, cut waste and improve 
efficiency, demonstrating that climate 
action and economic resilience can advance 
together. 
Several local community organisations, 
including Clondalkin Addiction Services 
Programme, Oakfield Trust, Round Towers 
GAA and ACE Enterprise Park, are leading 
the way with community climate action 
projects within the zone, including energy 
retrofits, solar PV installations and EV 
charging infrastructure. An electric Green 
Machine sweeper has been introduced as 
part of the council’s fleet decarbonisation 
programme, replacing a petrol‑powered 
unit previously used in the area. These 
initiatives demonstrate the impact 
of community led action in reducing 
emissions, enhancing local facilities and 
lowering energy costs. 
Clondalkin is also part of the Regions 
Putting Energy Efficiency First project, 
an Interreg Europe initiative launched in 
2025. Delivered locally in partnership 
with Dublin’s energy agency Codema, 
the project promotes the EU Energy 
Efficiency First principle by identifying 
barriers to improved energy efficiency and 
highlighting good practice. Engagement 
with stakeholders and councillors has 
helped shape a roadmap for future policy 
improvements, with the next phase 
focusing on shared learning with European 
partners to inform future updates of our 
Climate Action Plan. 
In addition, we continue to upgrade public 
lighting and retrofit social homes for 
better energy efficiency while the  the 
EnergyCloud pilot which delivers free 
hot water to social homes is also ongoing 
and further measures in Clondalkin, 
preparation for the launch of bike libraries 
this year, expansion of bike‑sharing options, 
development of an energy education 
programme for communities and the 
advancement of the Bawnogue District 
Enhancement Scheme, incorporating 
sustainable measures. 
Updates on climate action initiatives in 
the Clondalkin Decarbonising Zone and 
elsewhere in South Dublin are available at 
www.sdcc.ie/climateaction.

A new Litter Management Plan was 
adopted by the elected members of the 
council at the monthly meeting in April.  
The new plan, which is required under the 
Litter Pollution Acts, sets out how SDCC 
aims to meet our statutory obligation to 
address litter and illegal dumping. 
The process to update the Litter 
Management Plan began in February, with 
engagement through the Environment, 
Public Realm and Climate Change 
Strategic Policy Committee, followed 
by public consultation and review by the 
Circular Economy subcommittee of the 
SPC with the draft plan then subsequently 
recommended for adoption by the council  
at an  SPC meeting held on 30 March. 
The purpose of the Litter Management Plan 
is to outline a coordinated and strategic 
approach to tackling litter and illegal 
dumping. This includes enforcement and 
clean‑up measures, alongside a strong 
emphasis on prevention, awareness and 
community engagement. Addressing litter 
plays an important role in protecting the 
local environment, enhancing quality of life 
for residents and supporting the broader 
ambition of being a place that meets the 
needs and ambitions of everyone here now 
and in future. Reducing litter also helps 
ensure that public resources are used more 
effectively, as savings on on cleaning and 
illegal dumping can instead be directed 
towards improving our parks, open spaces 
and community facilities. 
The review of the previous plan highlighted 
a number of positive achievements 
including improved national cleanliness 
rankings, with Tallaght moving ten places 
up in the Irish Business Against Litter survey 
and improving from “Littered” to “Clean 
to European norms”. Over the period of 
the plan, solar‑powered compactor bins 
were installed at key locations, education 
and awareness initiatives were expanded 
through increased participation in the 
Green Schools Programme, and strong 
levels of community engagement were 
supported, with more than 660 clean‑up 
New Litter Management Plan approved 
Climate Leadership
and enhancement events held during  last 
year. Progress was also made with the 
introduction of an online graffiti reporting 
system, the installation of public drinking 
water stations to reduce plastic bottle 
waste, and the positive national impact of 
the Deposit Return Scheme in reducing 
common litter items such as cans and 
plastic bottles. 
Building on this progress, the new Litter 
Management Plan sets out clear objectives 
and priorities informed by the review 
process and public consultation. These 
include a stronger focus on litter prevention 
and circular economy principles, increased 
collaboration with stakeholders and the 
continued rollout of solar‑powered bin 
infrastructure. The plan also prioritises 
the expanded use of CCTV and other 
technologies to deter illegal dumping, 
enhanced engagement with fast‑food 
outlets to reduce packaging‑related litter, 
and clearer promotion of SDCC services 
and initiatives. 
Operational priorities within the plan 
include increasing the visibility of Litter 
Wardens, strengthening enforcement 
activity and improving our communication 
with local businesses and communities. 
Over the lifetime of the plan, further 
actions will include closer collaboration 
with schools and community groups 
on anti‑litter campaigns, alongside 
improvements to the design and 
appearance of our litter bin infrastructure. 
A continued emphasis on partnership and 
prevention underpins all actions identified 
in the plan. 
Public consultation played an important 
role in the development of the Litter 
Management Plan, with submissions 
considered as part of the Chief Executive’s 
Report. These contributions helped shape 
the final priorities and ensure the plan 
reflects the views and concerns of residents 
and stakeholders and which can be viewed 
on www.sdcc.ie.

Quality Housing
Free hot water for tenants through innovative wind energy scheme
A new initiative being delivered in 
partnership with EnergyCloud will provide 
free hot water to hundreds of council 
tenants through the use of surplus 
renewable energy. 
Following a successful pilot involving 
22 homes in Dunawley, the scheme is 
now being extended to more than 600 
properties across four estates: Tór an Rí, 
Buirg an Rí, Méile an Rí and Mac Uilliam. 
The scheme works by using surplus wind 
energy that would otherwise go to waste. 
A smart immersion controller is installed in 
each participating home, allowing excess 
renewable energy to be diverted directly 
to the household’s hot water tank. Tenants 
retain full control over their immersion at 
all times, and any energy costs incurred 
are refunded the following month, 
meaning hot water is provided at no cost 
to the household. 
Nationally, the scheme delivered free hot 
water on 117 nights in 2023, resulting 
in meaningful savings for participating 
households. Extending the programme 
locally supports tenants with cost‑of‑living 
pressures while also contributing to 
climate and sustainability goals. 
The initiative highlights the benefits of 
collaboration between local authorities, 
technology partners and communities, 
demonstrating how renewable energy 
can be used more efficiently to reduce 
household costs and support more 
sustainable living. 
Vacant Above the Shop Grant 
New funding has been announced by the 
Minister for Housing, Local Government 
and Heritage to support the reuse of 
vacant space in cities, towns and villages, 
including the Vacant Above the Shop 
Grant. The scheme aims to unlock unused 
space by converting vacant and derelict 
buildings, as well as unused areas above 
existing commercial premises, into homes. 
The Vacant Above the Shop Grant 
supports the refurbishment or conversion 
of vacant space above ground‑floor 
commercial premises, while retaining the 
commercial use at street level. Eligible 
properties must have been built before 
2008, be located in a city, town or village, 
and have upper floors that have been 
vacant for a minimum of two years. 
Grant funding of up to €95,000 is 
available for the refurbishment or 
conversion of the first above‑the‑shop 
unit. Additional funding of up to €20,000 
is available for a second unit, with a 
further €20,000 available where three 
or more units are created, subject to 
a maximum grant of €135,000 per 
building. Completed units may be used 
as a principal private residence or made 
available for rent. 
An Expert Advice Grant is also available 
to support owners before they apply for 
the Vacant Above the Shop Grant. This 
provides up to €5,000 towards the cost 
of professional advice on converting 
above‑the‑shop spaces or entire former 
commercial or public use buildings to 
residential use. The funding supports the 
preparation of an Expert Advice Report to 
help progress vacant properties towards 
reuse. 
Further information, including frequently 
asked questions and application forms, is 
available at www.sdcc.ie.

Quality Housing
The RAS Dublin pilot scheme is an 
enhanced Rental Accommodation Scheme 
designed to make it easier for private 
landlords to provide long‑term housing 
while supporting households in need of 
secure accommodation. The pilot offers a 
straightforward and reliable partnership with 
local authorities, combining long‑term letting 
arrangements, secure rental income and 
dedicated support throughout the tenancy. 
RAS provides stable, long‑term housing 
for eligible households through structured 
multi‑year agreements, rather than 
short‑term or emergency arrangements. 
SDCC, along with the other Dublin local 
authorities, works directly with private 
landlords to provide good‑quality homes for 
approved tenants, increasing the supply of 
secure housing options across the city. 
The scheme operates through a three‑way 
arrangement: landlords provide the property; 
the council pays the rent directly to the 
landlord and tenants are accommodated 
under normal tenancy arrangements.  
Guaranteed monthly rent removes the risk 
of missed payments or extended vacancy 
periods for landlords, while tenants benefit 
from long‑term security and homes that 
meet required safety and quality standards. 
Most agreements run for six to eight years, 
providing landlords with predictable and 
reliable income. Where a tenant leaves during 
the contract period, rent payments continue 
until a replacement RAS tenant is assigned. 
All participating properties must meet the 
RAS Dublin pilot scheme 
Housing (Standards for Rented Houses) 
Regulations 2019. Homes are inspected 
by the council before the tenancy begins 
and during the rental period. Landlords 
are required to maintain the property and 
insurance in line with standard private renting 
practices. Properties must also be registered 
with the Residential Tenancies Board, and 
landlords must hold valid tax clearance. 
Rent levels are determined by the local 
authority, taking account of local market 
evidence, comparable properties and the 
terms of the pilot scheme. Tenants pay rent 
to the council through the Differential Rent 
Scheme, ensuring a fair, transparent and 
consistent system for all parties. 
The RAS Dublin pilot scheme offers a range 
of benefits for landlords, including payment 
of up to 100% market rent, guaranteed rental 
income for the duration of the contract and 
continued payments during vacancy periods. 
There are no advertising costs, as tenants 
are sourced directly through the scheme. 
Landlords may also avail of front‑loaded rent 
payments where requested, financial support 
towards reinstatement costs at the end of 
the contract of up to three months’ rent, and 
access to 100% mortgage interest tax relief, 
subject to Revenue guidelines. 
For further information, landlords can contact 
the RAS Team by phone on 01-414 9000 or 
by email at ras@sdublincoco.ie.

A Thriving Economy
LEO Food and Drink Export Programme supports SME export growth 
LEO South Dublin’s Food and Drink 
Export Programme is a targeted support 
initiative designed to strengthen the 
export capacity of established Irish 
food and drink SMEs. The programme 
addresses a key capability gap within the 
sector by providing structured export 
training, market‑led planning and direct 
commercial engagement opportunities. 
The initiative aligns with national 
priorities, particularly in the context of 
continued growth in Ireland’s food and 
drink sector. With exports reaching a 
record €19 billion in 2025, global 
demand remains strong, highlighting the 
importance of supporting businesses to 
become export‑ready and scalable for 
international markets. 
This year, the second cohort of the 
programme will support 12 local food 
businesses. Participants will benefit 
from an integrated suite of professional 
development supports, including 
workshops, one‑to‑one mentoring, 
targeted market research and structured 
business development activity. Each 
business will also develop a tailored 
Export Development Plan to support its 
international growth ambitions. 
Additional supports include guidance on 
regulatory and logistics requirements, 
preparation of international sales 
materials and targeted advice focused 
on up to three priority export markets, 
ensuring companies are well prepared to 
enter or expand within overseas markets. 
To strengthen the programme’s 
commercial impact, each participating 
business will receive between 10 and 
15 qualified international sales leads, 
sourced through specialist networks. 
This ensures that capability building 
is directly linked to high‑value market 
access opportunities, supporting 
participants to translate strategic 
planning into tangible export outcomes.

Support for Clann Chrónáin tour guide training
The voluntary group Clann Chrónáin 
Tour Guides, based at Brú Chrónáin 
– the Clondalkin Round Tower Visitor 
Centre, continues to go from strength 
to strength. Since the centre opened 
in 2017, the group has worked in 
association with the Clondalkin Round 
Tower Heritage Group to deliver guided 
tours and share local history and heritage 
knowledge with visitors and the wider 
community. 
The group recently completed a 
structured training and upskilling 
programme for both existing and new 
volunteers. Delivered over an 11‑week 
period, much of the programme was 
led by the group’s long‑established 
volunteer guides, reflecting the depth of 
experience, expertise and commitment 
within the group across a wide range of 
local historical and cultural heritage 
topics. 
SDCC’s heritage programme supported 
this voluntary initiative by facilitating 
the involvement of external expertise to 
complement the in‑house programme. 
External contributors delivered 
best‑practice tour guide training and 
provided practical assessment and 
formative feedback, helping to maintain 
a consistently high standard of visitor 
experience. 
Clann Chrónáin continues to develop 
innovative ways to engage a wider 
audience, supporting increased footfall 
to Clondalkin and further strengthening 
Brú Chrónáin as an important cultural 
and heritage destination. 
A Thriving Economy
Work IQ Innovation Centre continues to support enterprise growth
Work IQ Innovation Centre continues to 
show steady growth and sustained levels 
of activity across its operations. The 
centre currently supports 36 businesses 
operating across a wide range of sectors, 
including pharmaceutical consulting, 
financial advisory services, software 
engineering, digital marketing, data 
design, leadership development, media 
and career coaching. Occupancy of the 
centre has increased to 59%, while the 
cumulative number of office licences 
issued now stands at 47. Since opening, 
the centre has supported the creation 
of 199 jobs, reflecting its ongoing role 
in supporting and facilitating local 
enterprise development.  
Oxford Innovation, who manage the 
centre on behalf of SDCC, continue to 
report a strong pipeline of interest and 
potential new occuapnts while feedback 
from prospective tenants has informed 
the design of a new coworking space, 
which is currently in development to 
respond to evolving workspace needs. 
Engagement with external partners has 
continued to progress. Collaborative 
work with Tallaght University Hospital 
and Technological University Dublin 
is advancing, while discussions with 
additional potential partners are 
ongoing.  
The centre also plays an active role 
within the local innovation ecosystem. 
Recent activity has included hosting 
the launch of the South Dublin County 
Council Economic Strategy and 
facilitating a range of events as part of 
Local Enterprise Week which included 
sessions delivered by South Dublin 
Partnership and Startup Network 
Europe as well as  LEO mentoring 
clinics, training programmes, and 
network meetings, export programme 
sessions as Work IQ continues to 
develop as a space that is integral 
to engagement by local businesses, 
entrepreneurs and innovators.

The review of the Eastern and Midland 
Regional Assembly’s Regional Spatial 
and Economic Strategy has formally 
commenced, marking an important 
statutory process to update the 
long‑term spatial and economic 
framework for the region. 
The review process began on 26 March 
with the publication of a Strategic 
Issues Paper. This paper sets out the 
key challenges, opportunities and 
strategic questions facing the region and 
provides the basis for an initial pre‑draft 
public consultation. This stage of 
consultation offers an early opportunity 
for communities, stakeholders, local 
authorities and public bodies to help 
inform the direction of the revised 
strategy. Public consultation on the 
Strategic Issues Paper will remain open 
until 22 May. 
Submissions received during this 
pre‑draft consultation will inform the 
preparation of a draft Regional Spatial 
and Economic Strategy, which will be 
published at a later stage for statutory 
public consultation. 
As a long‑term strategy guiding regional 
growth and development, the Regional 
Spatial and Economic Strategy is of 
strategic importance to South Dublin 
and the wider region. It sits within the 
planning hierarchy beneath the National 
Planning Framework – First Revision 
and will provide a key framework for 
the preparation of the next County 
Development Plan. Implementation 
of the strategy is progressed through 
coordinated engagement between local 
authorities, Government Departments 
and relevant public bodies, aligning 
spatial planning and economic 
development around the core principles 
of healthy placemaking, climate action 
and economic opportunity. This work 
A Better Place
builds on progress made under the first 
Regional Spatial and Economic Strategy 
adopted in 2019. 
The Planning and Development Act 
2024 requires that the review of 
the Regional Spatial and Economic 
Strategy is completed in advance of 
the commencement of reviews of new 
ten‑year County Development Plans. 
Further legislation is expected to 
provide a mechanism to postpone the 
commencement of County Development 
Plan reviews, allowing timelines to align 
with the requirements of the new Act.

Oldcastle Drive playspace 
Funding secured through the Department 
of Housing, Local Government and 
Heritage under the Dormant Accounts 
Fund will support measures that enhance 
tenancy sustainment and community 
development within Traveller‑specific 
group housing schemes and halting sites. 
This funding provides for a range of 
initiatives, including the development 
of play areas within Traveller‑specific 
accommodation. These spaces 
are designed to create safer, more 
engaging environments for children, 
supporting wellbeing, development and 
opportunities for active play. 
Following extensive consultation with 
residents of Oldcastle Drive in Clondalkin, 
along with engagement among a range 
of teams in the council, our Traveller 
Accommodation Unit submitted an 
application to DHLGH for support for 
the new playspace. We were delighted 
to recently receive notification that 
this application was successful for 
a playspace which will enhance the 
day‑to‑day environment for children living 
in Oldcastle Drive, promoting inclusion 
and active play. The design will reflect 
Traveller traditions and has been informed 
by similar projects delivered successfully 
elsewhere in the county. This investment 
represents a welcome addition to the 
community and will provide lasting 
benefits for children and families in the 
area.

Historic Structures Fund 2026 support for Peamount Hospital 
A Better Place
Peamount Hospital has been awarded 
€90,108 under the Historic Structures 
Fund to support conservation works 
to St Finian’s former schoolhouse, a 
timber‑clad, timber‑frame building 
constructed in 1935 to designs by 
Beckett and Harrington Architects. 
The Historic Structures Fund is provided 
by the Department of Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage and is 
administered locally by tour Architectural 
Conservation team. The fund supports 
the repair and reuse of historic buildings 
where projects demonstrate a clear 
residential or community benefit. 
The allocation will support continued 
conservation works to the external fabric 
of the building as part of its adaptive 
reuse for community purposes within the 
wider hospital complex. This marks the 
third consecutive year of support under 
the fund for the project, following awards 
of approximately €180,000 in 2024 and 
2025 for earlier phases of conservation 
works. 
The continued investment will help 
protect the architectural and historical 
significance of the former schoolhouse 
while supporting its long‑term 
sustainable use as a community asset. 
Whitestown Greenway 
Work is now almost complete on the 
Whitestown Greenway, which will create 
a new green infrastructure corridor 
along the Whitestown Stream between 
Killinarden Park and Sean Walsh Park. 
The project is expected to be finished 
this month providing approximately 640 
metres of new pedestrian and cycle 
infrastructure. The route has an important 
interconnecting function within the wider 
cycling and walking network, linking with 
a combination of existing, approved and 
planned schemes, including the Dodder 
Greenway, the Citywest to Rathfarnham 
cycle scheme and the N81 cycle scheme. 
The greenway will also connect to the 
Dublin Mountains Way trailhead. 
Public lighting is being installed along 
the length of the route, with a design that 
allows lights to dim during periods of 
non‑use to accommodate bats travelling 
along the Whitestown Stream corridor. 
The scheme also includes 24‑hour CCTV 
coverage and a controlled pedestrian 
crossing at Whitestown Drive, enhancing 
safety and accessibility for users. 
The project has an overall construction 
cost of approximately €2 million, 
with €300,000 in funding support 
provided through the Department of 
Rural and Community Development 
and the Gaeltacht’s Outdoor Recreation 
Infrastructure Scheme.

Connected Communities
Bealtaine festival events
Local community groups and centres 
are being supported to deliver a varied 
programme of Bealtaine activities 
throughout the month, celebrating 
creativity, culture and positive ageing 
while encouraging people to stay socially 
connected and active. 
A wide range of organisations are 
taking part, with events designed to 
promote wellbeing, lifelong learning and 
community participation. Firhouse Active 
Age will host a series of Lust for Life 
events alongside creative workshops in 
Firhouse Community Centre. The Park 
Community Centre will offer outdoor 
Tai Chi sessions, weather permitting, 
followed by refreshments and live music, 
as well as a flower-arranging workshop. 
Buadáin le Gaeilge will host a Féile 
Bealtaine singing session open to all, 
while Belgard Community Centre will 
feature performances by Belgard’s Trad 
Group and Boland’s School of Dance. 
Additional initiatives include a Bealtaine 
event hosted by the Cara Café Dementia 
Café in Ballyroan Community Centre. 
Esker Active Retirement is taking part 
in a four-week health and wellbeing 
programme, while Ballyowen Community 
Centre is hosting a schedule of activities 
in partnership with Ballyowen Women’s 
Group, including Tai Chi, chair yoga and 
engagement with the local Historical 
Society. 
North Clondalkin Library will run a 
month-long programme featuring Making 
Memories workshops, calligraphy classes, 
a Bealtaine Movie Club, a My Fair Lady 
sing-along and a genealogy session 
facilitated by Cathy Scuffle. A tea dance 
taking place on 20 May will be the 
library’s flagship Bealtaine event. 
For more information, or to find out 
what is happening in your local area, 
contact your local community centre 
or community officer by emailing 
community@sdublincoco.ie. 
Time Capsule launch at North Clondalkin Library
The Time Capsule Sessions are an 
interview series that records the 
experiences of people who moved to 
the North Clondalkin area from the 
1970s onwards. Through in‑depth 
conversations, participants reflect on 
what brought them to the area and 
the memories and moments that have 
shaped their lives over time. Each 
interview contributes to a shared record 
of North Clondalkin’s social history. 
The project has culminated in a 
photographic exhibition now on display 
at North Clondalkin Library. The 
exhibition brings together each recorded 
account with a portrait of the participant, 
captured by award‑winning photographer 
and Humans of Dublin creator Peter 
Varga. 
The exhibition was officially launched by 
Mayor Cllr. Pamela Kearns on Monday 
30 March. The launch event brought 
together participants, local residents and 
community partners to recognise the 
contributors and mark the opening of the 
exhibition. 
The Time Capsule Sessions exhibition is 
open to the public at North Clondalkin 
Library and invites visitors to explore the 
personal stories and shared experiences 
that have helped shape the identity of 
the area.

Event for local Special Olympics athletes 
On Monday 27 April, we were delighted 
to welcome 84 local Special Olympics 
athletes to Tallaght Stadium to mark 
their upcoming participation in the 
Ireland Summer Games 2026. The 
games are expected to attract over 
1,200 athletes, along with many 
coaches, family members, volunteers and 
spectators, across four days of activity in 
venues around Dublin from 18–21 June. 
The summer games event will officially 
start with an opening ceremony in 
Tallaght Stadium on 18 June, so 
the recent event was also a great 
opportunity to give a preview of the 
facility to the athletes and their coaches 
and family members. 
On the evening athletes spoke about 
their anticipation for the games as they 
reflected on the scale of the occasion 
while Mayor of South Dublin, Cllr. 
Pamela Kearns praised their achievement 
in reaching the national finals and 
described them as strong ambassadors 
for the county. 
The CEO of Special Olympics Ireland, 
Karen Coventry, thanked SDCC for 
organising the event for the local 
athletes and said the games will have 
a positive impact on athletes and their 
communities. 
To stay informed on the Ireland Summer 
Games 2026, visit www.specialolympics.
ie. 
Connected Communities
Young people took part in a multi‑agency 
road safety workshop on 20 March, 
aimed at raising awareness of the dangers 
associated with e‑scooters, scramblers 
and unsafe road use. The interactive 
session brought together emergency 
services and healthcare professionals to 
provide practical, real‑world learning. 
The workshop was organised in 
collaboration with the South Dublin 
Junior Safety Forum and took place in 
Tallaght, with representatives from An 
Garda Síochána, Dublin Fire Brigade and 
Children’s Health Ireland in attendance. 
Students learned about the potential 
consequences of road traffic incidents 
and gained insight into the roles played by 
emergency responders. 
An Garda Síochána and Dublin Fire Brigade 
delivered a simulated incident involving 
a young woman who had been thrown 
from an e‑scooter. Students observed the 
coordinated response as the scene was 
secured, the situation assessed and urgent 
medical care provided. The demonstration 
emphasised the importance of rapid 
response, teamwork and safety awareness 
during emergencies. 
Providing a clinical perspective, Dr 
Donnelly from Children’s Health Ireland, 
alongside Clinical Nurse Specialist 
Orla Stavely, spoke to students about 
the injuries commonly treated in the 
emergency department as a result of 
e‑scooter and bicycle collisions. They 
outlined the often serious and long‑term 
impacts of these incidents, reinforcing the 
importance of protective measures and 
responsible behaviour on the roads. 
Students were also given the opportunity 
to speak directly with emergency service 
personnel and ask questions about making 
safer choices when using e‑scooters, 
scramblers and sharing the road with other 
users. 
The workshop reinforced the importance 
of education, prevention and shared 
responsibility in keeping roads safe, while 
also highlighting the vital work carried out 
daily by emergency services. The South 
Dublin Junior Safety Forum continues to 
promote safety awareness among young 
people, supporting safer decision‑making 
across the county.

programme and artist line‑up for RePlay,

Artificial intelligence literacy training
As part of its people‑first and 
safe‑by‑design approach to artificial 
intelligence, SDCC is continuing to take 
practical steps to support the responsible 
use of AI tools across the organisation. 
Building on established governance 
arrangements, human oversight and 
strong data protection practices, Digital 
Services has launched an AI literacy 
programme to help staff safely explore 
how AI can support everyday work. 
This work continues to align with the 
EU Artificial Intelligence Act and the 
Council’s commitment to maintaining 
public trust. 
To date, 82 staff members have taken 
part in AI literacy training. The sessions 
use clear language and practical 
examples to show how AI tools can 
support efficiency and day‑to‑day tasks, 
while reinforcing that people remain fully 
in control of decisions and outputs at all 
times. 
An initial session focused on building a 
shared understanding of what artificial 
intelligence is and how it can be used 
responsibly in a local authority setting. A 
follow‑on session then explored practical 
applications, demonstrating how AI tools 
can support everyday work within familiar 
office environments, while emphasising 
careful handling of information. 
This ongoing programme will help 
build staff confidence and capability, 
supporting the safe and considered 
adoption of artificial intelligence while 
keeping people, trust and public service 
values at the centre of the organisation’s 
approach.
As part of the ongoing Cyber Security 
Programme, Digital Services delivered a 
week‑long programme of cyber security 
awareness events for staff from 13 to 17 
April 2026. Cyber Security Awareness 
Week focused on a clear and consistent 
message that keeping the organisation 
safe is a shared responsibility. 
Across the week, staff recorded a total 
of 931 attendances, reflecting a strong 
and encouraging level of engagement. 
This participation provides confidence 
that key messages are resonating 
and that safer digital habits are being 
reinforced across the organisation. 
Sessions explored how many 
cyber‑attacks operate and highlighted 
that people, rather than systems, are 
often the primary target. Common 
tactics such as applying pressure, 
creating false urgency or impersonating 
trusted contacts were examined. Staff 
were encouraged to slow down, think 
before acting and make safe decisions as 
part of the organisation’s human firewall. 
The sessions also reinforced that while 
technology enables more effective ways 
of working, it can introduce new risks. 
Simple everyday habits, clear processes 
and consistent ways of working play 
an important role in protecting people, 
systems and data. Cyber security is most 
effective when everyone remains alert 
and takes shared responsibility. 
Throughout the week, staff had 
opportunities to ask questions and 
receive practical advice, helping 
to embed security awareness into 
day‑to‑day work. An online performance 
of Hooked demonstrated how easily 
mistakes can happen under pressure and 
highlighted the importance of awareness 
in preventing incidents. 
Real‑world examples of cyber incidents 
from other organisations illustrated 
the serious impact of phishing and 
ransomware attacks, while also 
reinforcing that early reporting can 
prevent issues from escalating. 
The key messages from the week were 
clear: pause before responding to 
unexpected requests, trust instincts 
when something feels wrong, and report 
concerns immediately, even if a mistake 
may have been made.

100% of our road fleet now decarbonised 
We operate a fleet of more than 300 
vehicles with a target under our Climate 
Action Plan to decarbonise a minimum of 
31% of this by 2030 to support corporate 
emission‑reduction targets and national 
climate obligations.  Supporting this overall 
target, we embarked on an ambitious 
approach to achieve full decarbonisation of 
our road fleet. 
This started in 2024 with the introduction 
of a pilot project to trial the use of 
Hydrogenated Vegetable Oil (HVO) in some 
of our fleet as an alternative to conventional 
road diesel. HVO is a renewable fuel that 
delivers significant lifecycle greenhouse 
gas emissions reductions compared with 
fossil diesel. Following the successful 
completion of the pilot, HVO has now been 
rolled out across 100% of our road‑going 
diesel vehicles. This has enabled emissions 
reductions on vehicles where there is not 
yet a viable electric alternative, delivering 
results well in advance of expectations. 
To further embed low‑carbon operational 
practices, two new winter maintenance 
vehicles have been procured that will 
operate exclusively on HVO. These vehicles 
are currently under fabrication and are 
scheduled for delivery later this year, 
ensuring that specialised winter services 
align with the same decarbonisation 
standards as the wider fleet. 
Alongside this transition, we continue to 
prioritise further procurement of electric 
vehicles where operationally appropriate. 
In addition to reducing emissions and 
lowering operating costs, electric vehicles 
deliver wider benefits for air quality and 
noise reduction in communities.  Last year, 
eight electric vehicles were acquired to 
replace internal combustion engine vehicles 
on a direct one‑for‑one basis while in the 
first quarter of this year, two large electric 
vans were delivered, with delivery of a 
further six medium electric vans expected 
this month. These additions will increase 
electric vehicles to 11% of our overall fleet 
County Matters
with further investment planned over the 
next two years. 
Operational equipment is also being 
decarbonised where feasible with two 
electric Green Machine pedestrian 
sweepers recently introduced for use in 
Clondalkin and Lucan. These sweepers 
contribute to emissions reductions in 
non‑road mobile machinery while also 
improving air quality in public spaces. 
To support the expanding electric fleet, 
investment is underway to deliver a network 
of designated depot charging points. A 
tender for the installation of depot‑based 
charging infrastructure is scheduled to be 
published during the summer. This project 
is a key enabler for the continued transition 
to electric vehicles and will be delivered 
across several depots. 
In parallel, upgrades have already been 
implemented to existing charging 
infrastructure at council depots to increase 
capacity, reduce charging turnaround times 
and improve reporting on electric vehicle 
utilisation and operational efficiency. 
Construction of a new mechanical 
depot, designed specifically to support 
the maintenance of electric vehicles, 
commenced last month. This facility will 
enable proactive servicing and support 
by the Mechanical Services team as the 
electric fleet continues to grow. 
The transition from fossil diesel to 
electric vehicles, combined with the full 
substitution of road diesel with HVO, 
means that the Council has effectively 
decarbonised its road‑going fleet. This 
means that we have effectively already 
exceeded our original Climate Action 
Plan target of 31% fleet decarbonisation 
by 2030 and represents a significant 
contribution to overall emissions reduction , 
with additional benefits for local air quality.

Public consultation has been undertaken 
on the draft City Edge Strategic Urban 
Regeneration Framework, which sets out 
a statutory planning approach of City 
Edge within the SDCC administrative 
area. The framework builds on the vision 
and delivery strategy established in the 
City Edge Strategic Framework adopted 
in 2022 and provides detailed guidance 
to support future development. 
The Strategic Urban Regeneration 
Framework identifies a number of Priority 
Development Areas where mixed‑use 
regeneration will be focused in the short 
to medium term. These areas account 
for approximately 28% of the City Edge 
lands within our area with the potential 
to deliver around 9,000 new homes and 
support up to 12,000 jobs. 
The overall vision for City Edge is to 
create a connected, green and inclusive 
mixed‑use urban quarter that supports 
healthier living, stronger communities and 
a more sustainable and climate‑resilient 
future. 
The draft framework is proposed as a 
Variation to the South Dublin County 
Development Plan 2022–2028 
and is accompanied by the required 
environmental assessments and transport 
modelling reports.  
Submissions could be made until 12 
May after which, a Chief Executive’s 
Report will be prepared summarising 
the submissions received and providing 
responses to the issues raised. Elected 
members will then consider the report 
and decide whether to adopt the 
proposed Variation, with or without 
modifications, or to reject it.

The completion of the Annual Financial 
Statement (AFS), which was noted at the 
council meeting last month, marks an 
important milestone for the organisation 
and provides an opportunity for reflection 
on our financial performance. Overall, it 
shows strong and resilient performance 
for the financial year ending 31 December 
2025. Despite challenges from wider 
economic conditions, inflationary costs 
and sector-specific volatility, maintaining 
effective financial controls allowed us to 
retain focus on our strategic objectives 
and supported continued delivery of high-
quality services. The year‑end position 
highlights the importance of continued 
financial discipline, particularly in the 
context of inflationary pressures and 
wider external uncertainty. 
Small revenue account surplus 
demonstrates narrow operating margins 
Revenue expenditure amounted to 
€392.9 million which was 0.25%, above 
budget, reflecting the tight margins in 
our day‑to‑day operations.  With income 
broadly matching expenditure, our closing 
surplus was just €24,002 resulting in an 
accumulated revenue reserve of €12.39 
million at year‑end.  
Continued capital investment at scale 
Capital expenditure totalled €333.6 
million, reflecting continued investment 
in acquisition, construction and 
enhancement of significant fixed assets, 
supported by income of €302.3 million 
before transfers from the revenue 
account of €47.5 million.  This means 
that our capital account finished the 
year with an overall positive movement 
of €18.8 million, ensuring that we are 
well positioned to continue delivery of 
hosuign, infrastructure and amentieis 
to build on the achievements of 2025 
which saw completion of 812 social 
homes, exceeding the target of 772, 
alongside continued energy‑efficiency 
upgrades, active travel schemes, strategic 
infrastructure at Clonburris SDZ, and 
multiple community and parks projects as 
part of our broader capital programme. 
€3.7 billion fixed asset base 
Our fixed assets net book value was 
€3.7 billion at year end. This includes 
operational assets valued at €2.5 billion 
and infrastructural assets of €1.1 billion, 
reflecting the scale of our service delivery 
and infrastructure responsibility while 
community assets valued at €27 million 
and non‑operational assets of €89.2 
million made up the remainder of our 
asset base. 
Improved debtor position reflects 
collection performance trajectory 
Our financial statement also shows 
a continued reduction in monies 
outstanding to the council as our 
collection rates improved.  Of particular 
note, commercial rates collection 
reached 95% with arrears reduced to 
€11.1 million, the lowest level recorded 
since 2008, while the marginal increase 
in housing loan arrears was due to 
capitalisation of some customer credit 
balances. 
Managing risk and uncertainty going 
forward 
Looking ahead, while our relatively strong 
financial position presents opportunities 
to continue to invest in local services 
and infrastructure, wider economic 
issues including energy market volatility 
and inflationary pressures necessitate 
continued vigilance. Maintaining reserves 
and delivering core services will require 
ongoing control of both revenue and 
capital expenditure, while responding 
to continued demands for housing, 
infrastructure and community investment. 
The work of all staff involved in 
ensuring the completeness, accuracy 
and timeliness of the AFS as well as 
ongoing financial management across all 
workstreams is greatly appreciated and 
ensures that the council has the platform 
to continue to create greater opportunity 
for all in South Dublin.

The Minister for the Department of 
Housing, Local Government and Heritage 
marked a significant milestone in the 
delivery of the Clonburris Strategic 
Development Zone (SDZ) with the official 
ribbon cutting of the first completed 
section of Stage 1B of the South Link 
Street on Wednesday, 29th of April.
The event was attended by 
representatives from the Department 
of Housing, Local Government and 
Heritage including Minister James 
Browne, the Urban Regeneration and 
Development Fund (URDF) Team, the 
Mayor of South Dublin, Cllr. Pamela 
Kearns, SDCC Director of Services for 
Planning and Transport Eoin Burke and 
the SDCC Planning and Delivery Team, 
Design Teams, Project Managers, private 
landowners and the main contractor 
Clonmel.
The South Link Street is a key piece of 
infrastructure, comprising approximately 
4km of new east–west roadway, including 
junction upgrades, drainage, water 
services, landscaping and parkland. It is 
a critical element in unlocking lands for 
housing delivery across the SDZ.
The event marked the opening of the first 
completed section of Stage 1B of the 
South Link Street, building on the earlier 
delivery of Stage 1A, which is already 
operational.
Further sections of Stage 1B will open 
on a phased and incremental basis over 
the coming years, aligned with adjacent 
housing delivery and the reduction of 
construction activity. This approach 
ensures that the infrastructure can be 
brought into use safely while supporting 
the continued development of the wider 
Clonburris area.
Located less than 15 minutes by rail from 
Dublin City Centre, Clonburris is one of 
the largest regeneration and housing 
opportunities in the country. The area 
has the capacity to deliver approximately 
9,500 new homes, alongside 90 hectares 
of parks, schools, community facilities 
and high-quality public realm, supporting 
a future population of over 23,000 
people.
Clonburris represents a flagship example 
of compact, sustainable development 
aligned with the National Planning 
Framework (First Revision 2025) and the 
Government’s national housing strategy, 
Delivering Homes, Building Communities 
2025-2030: An Action Plan on Housing 
Supply and Targeting Homelessness. 
The project supports delivery targets set 
out in SDCC’s Housing Delivery Action 
Plan 2022–2026, demonstrating how 
coordinated national investment can 
accelerate housing delivery in strategic, 
well-connected locations.
As of Q4 2025, substantial progress has 
been made in housing delivery across 
the Clonburris SDZ, with 4,231 homes 
granted planning permission, 3,106 
homes under construction and 1,419 
homes completed, of which 1,014 are 
already occupied. The development 
includes a mix of social, affordable, cost 
rental and private housing.
The project highlights the strong 
collaboration between SDCC, the 
Department of Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage, the National 
Transport Authority, Clonburris 
Infrastructure Ltd and key landowners 
including Cairn Homes, Kelland Homes 
and Evara.
This milestone represents a significant 
step forward in the transformation of 
Clonburris into a vibrant, well-connected 
and sustainable new community. 
Continued investment in infrastructure 
will support the ongoing delivery of 
housing and community amenities in the 
years ahead.

sustainable development and high‑quality 
public spaces. Together, these initiatives

the council’s key priorities.

brings together sport, leisure, childcare

accessible setting. 
Delivered in phases, the campus now 
combines a new purpose‑built swimming 
pool with the refurbishment of the 
existing leisure centre. The new building 
facility includes a 25- metre pool 
alongside a separate multi‑use pool with 
a movable floor, allowing for a wide range 
of activities. Supporting facilities such 
as a sauna and steam room wellbeing 
suite, exercise rooms, and flexible studios 
provide opportunities for both structured 
programmes and casual use. A welcoming 
entrance space with café encourages 
social interaction and connection around 
shared activities.

home for Esker Boxing Club, as well 
as a crèche and secure outdoor play 
area. A new changing pavilion, nearing 
completion, will support field sports 
users in Griffeen Valley Park. The campus 
has been designed to a high energy 
standard, supporting sustainable building 
practices while delivering long‑term 
community benefits.

Lucan are also visible within the historic 
core of the village, where the reopening 
of Lucan Village Green has created a new 
social focal point for local communities 
and visitors alike. Located between the 
Griffeen River, Main Street, Lucan Road 
and Dispensary Lane, the renewed space 
provides a central gathering place within 
the village. 
The redesigned green includes seating 
areas, a bandstand, access to the river, 
amphitheatre‑style seating and new 
planting, creating a welcoming and 
flexible space that can be enjoyed 
throughout the day. The layout supports 
both everyday use and larger community 
events, contributing to the vitality of the 
village centre. 
This work is complemented by wider 
public realm improvements, including 
enhanced access to Lucan Demesne, 
upgrades to the Liffey Weir promenade 
and refurbishment works to Lucan

Bridge. Together, these projects improve 
connectivity, accessibility and the overall 
appearance of the village, supporting 
stronger links between natural, historic 
and civic spaces. 
  
A further key element of Lucan’s 
transformation is the opening of Lucan 
House and Demesne to the public. 
Following a pilot trial opening phase, the 
grounds now provide controlled access 
for visitors to experience the landscape, 
biodiversity and heritage of this historic 
site. 
The demesne is undergoing a phased 
programme of conservation and 
restoration works, designed to protect 
its architectural and environmental 
significance while improving access over 
time. Information boards across the 
site provide insight into its historic use 
and ongoing conservation approach, 
helping visitors to connect with the area’s 
heritage. 
Public access is currently managed to 
ensure safety, protect sensitive features 
and support ongoing works. While some 
areas remain restricted, the phased 
opening offers an early opportunity to 
experience the space and understand the 
long‑term vision being developed through 
the emerging masterplan. 
Taken together, these projects reflect 
a clear and consistent approach to 
place‑making, focusing on quality design, 
sustainability and community need. 
Investment in sports facilities supports 
active lifestyles and wellbeing, while 
enhanced public spaces encourage 
social interaction and local activity. 
Conservation works ensure that Lucan’s 
heritage is protected and integrated into 
its future development. 
These improvements also support wider 
strategic goals, including healthier 
communities, sustainable infrastructure 
and economic vitality. By strengthening 
connections between public facilities, 
green spaces and the village centre, 
Lucan is evolving as a more accessible, 
inclusive and resilient place. 
As these projects continue to develop and 
mature, they demonstrate the value of 
coordinated investment in shaping places 
that work for people, support community 
life and respond to future needs. 
Lucan’s ongoing transformation reflects 
a long‑term commitment to creating 
high‑quality environments that enhance 
everyday life across the county.
